newsitem.title: USA: N.C. tobacco order does not affect other judges.
newsitem.headline: N.C. tobacco order does not affect other judges.

text.p: A temporary court order barring distribution of Ligget Group tobacco documents does not prevent judges from outside North Carolina from reviewing the Ligget papers in private, a lawyer from Philip Morris Cos said.

The lawyer from Philip Morris Cos said in a Florida court hearing that the North Carolina Judge in Winston-Salem who last week issued the temporary restraining order late Wednesday amended that order to make clear he was not trying to prevent private review of the Ligget papers by other judges overseeing lawsuits filed against U.S. tobacco companies.

The Liggett group documents were made available last Thursday as part of a sweeping deal between Liggett Group, a unit of Brooke Group, and 22 state governments suing the tobacco industry to recover an estimated $30 billion in costs spent treating sick smokers.

In exchange for settling claims against itself, Liggett agreed to provide internal industry documents which anti-tobacco lawyers have said will prove tobacco companies have long hid the danger of smoking from Americans.

Tobacco company lawyers last Thursday secured a restraining order in the North Carolina Court preventing wide distribution of the papers, claiming that some of the documents were protected by client-lawyer privilege.
A hearing on the restraining order is scheduled for Monday morning in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.
Lawyers pressing anti-tobacco lawsuits in Illinois on Monday, won court orders requiring Liggett to turn over the papers to judges there.
Attorneys representing the state of Florida have also asked the judge overseeing its case against tobacco companies to require Liggett to deliver the papers to a West Palm Beach Court.

Murray Garnick, the lawyer for Philip Morris, said the North Carolina order was meant to prevent the access of reporters and other non-judicial organizations to the papers before they were examined by a trial judge.
Garnick said the tobacco companies wanted to insure that documents concerning their clients were not unfairly made public.
